clue.text: Rather too much from a flat out confection

indicators.note: a confection is something concocted or mixed up, so the words before it are cooked into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A pastry chef's 'flat out' creation is far too rich.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle's clues are rhyming couplets: this line rhymes with 2 Down's. 'Confection' looks like the dessert but signals the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something to a fault means doing it excessively, carrying a virtue too far.

clue.text: The French, below average in every direction

definitions.note: loose: a parallel line keeps the same course whichever way it is followed

indicators.note: in a down light, being below means coming later in the column, so the French article is placed last

blocks.note: par is the standard or average score
every one is all
le is the masculine French for 'the', here turned around

explanation.surface: The French are rated below average on every count.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is a best guess: 'below' sets the French article after the rest in this down light, and it reads backwards with no clear signal; the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Parallel lines run alike all along their length, keeping equal distance in each direction they extend.

clue.text: Rat that you'll find in canals in Geelong

indicators.note: what you find inside a run of words is sitting there already, spelt across their boundary

blocks.note: spans the end of canals, the word in, and the start of Geelong

explanation.surface: A rodent spotted in the waterways of an Australian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Geelong is a port city near Melbourne. 'Rat' looks like the animal but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To rat and to sing are both slang for informing on someone to the police.

clue.text: Two lines are padding inferior song

indicators.note: padding stuffs something inside, so the first letters sit within the word for inferior

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for line, twice
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
inferior quality is bad

explanation.surface: A poor song stretched out with a couple of filler lines.
explanation.walkthrough: The three letters from the first words go inside BAD after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballad is a narrative song or poem, often sentimental, so it is a kind of song.

clue.text: Returned a dessert, an inedible sponge

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so the next words are read from the end

blocks.note: taken as written
a fool is a fruit-and-cream pudding

explanation.surface: A diner sends back a pudding that turned out to be sponge cake fit only for washing.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is a British dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream; 'sponge' tempts toward cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A loofah is the dried fibrous pod of a gourd used as a bath scrubber, a sponge nobody eats.

clue.text: Player miscast now and then for 18s?

definitions.note: loose: lyrics are where rhymes are put

indicators.note: now and then means only occasionally, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of the two words

explanation.surface: An actor in the wrong role occasionally fluffs the rhyming lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is RHYME, so the definition asks for words that carry rhymes; the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Song lyrics are the words set to music, and that is where rhyming couplets usually live.

clue.text: Son, family nut, hairless oaf dressed in grunge

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
one's kin are one's family
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A family's son has become a shaven-headed lout in scruffy clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' looks like a crazy person in the family but is slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinhead is a youth with a shaved head, associated with a rough, aggressive subculture and its clothing.

clue.text: Crude antisepsis lacks power, but cleans

indicators.note: lacking something means it is missing, so a letter drops out of the word
crude means rough and unrefined, so the letters are in a raw, unsorted state

blocks.note: taken as written
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A rough-and-ready disinfecting method is weak but still does the job.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the P from the fodder before shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: To sanitise is to make hygienic by removing germs, which is to clean thoroughly.

clue.text: Fellow will ring for a "how do you do?"

blocks.note: a fellow is a male, he
'll is the contraction of will
O is round like a ring

explanation.surface: A man will phone to say good day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call but gives the round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are polite greetings on meeting someone, so one can stand in for the other.

clue.text: Standard of length and rhythm that's observed throughout except in this particular clue

definitions.text: rhythm that's observed throughout except in this particular clue

blocks.note: first meaning: the SI base unit of distance

blocks.clueFragment: rhythm that's observed throughout except in this particular clue
blocks.note: second meaning: the regular beat of verse, which every other line here keeps and this long one breaks

explanation.walkthrough: Every clue in this puzzle is a line of rhyming verse with a steady beat; this sprawling one deliberately has none, a joke on itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A metre is both a unit of length of a hundred centimetres and the rhythmic pattern of stresses in poetry.

clue.text: Words oft repeated conveying "Forbear!"

blocks.note: first meaning: the chorus that recurs in a song or poem
second meaning: the imperative 'hold back'

explanation.walkthrough: One word is both a noun for a chorus and a verb meaning to abstain, here as a command.
explanation.definitionFit: A refrain is a recurring chorus, and to refrain is to forbear, to stop oneself from acting.

clue.text: I allege, unreliably, Jesus was there

indicators.note: an unreliable account cannot be trusted to keep things in their true order

blocks.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A doubtful witness claims Jesus was present.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a sceptic's claim; the definition is a place, not an event.
explanation.definitionFit: Galilee is the region of northern Israel where, in the Gospels, Jesus grew up and preached.

clue.text: Poetry item with myths at the core

indicators.note: the core of something is its centre, so only the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: a pair of lovers is an item, a couple
the central letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A piece of verse built around ancient legends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poetry item' reads as one phrase, but 'item' is the romantic pair and 'Poetry' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A couplet is a pair of rhyming lines of verse, a small unit of poetry, like each clue here.

clue.text: Supplier of spam left in snack? I'm not sure

indicators.note: in puts one thing inside another, here inside the word for snack

blocks.note: a snack is a bit of food
L is the abbreviation for left
er is a hesitant noise of uncertainty

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the tinned meat was left in their lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: Spam is the tinned meat in the surface but junk email in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who floods inboxes with unwanted messages is supplying spam, the junk email kind.

clue.text: Push on a jumper with first part of spring

blocks.note: a frog is an animal that jumps
March is the first month of spring in the northern hemisphere

explanation.surface: Putting on a sweater at the start of spring.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is British for a sweater, which the surface uses; the wordplay wants something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: To frogmarch someone is to force them forward by holding their arms, pushing them along.

clue.text: Sounding outstanding, a multifoot thing

indicators.note: sounding means as it is heard spoken, not as it is written

blocks.note: a debt that is outstanding is still owed

explanation.surface: Something that sounds superb, with many feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise but means unpaid; a 'foot' is a metrical unit of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: An ode is a lyric poem, and its lines are made of metrical feet, so it is a thing of many feet.

clue.text: High crimes at last with Conservatives' lies

indicators.note: at last points to the final position, so only the end letter is kept

blocks.note: high and tall are synonyms
the final letter
the Tories are Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Political misdeeds topped by the Conservatives' lying.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories is the everyday name for members of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall stories are exaggerated, unbelievable tales, so they are lies of a sort.

clue.text: Televise tune with look that's inspired

blocks.note: first meaning: to broadcast
second meaning: a melody
further meanings: an appearance or manner, and what is breathed in

explanation.walkthrough: Several senses of one short word are piled up: broadcast, melody, manner, and the stuff of breathing, which is what 'inspired' means literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers broadcasting a programme, a simple melody, a person's manner, and the atmosphere we inhale.

clue.text: Popular stage routine I have retired?

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
a performer's act is their routine
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A comedian with a well-loved routine wonders if it is time to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: the retired are no longer active.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone retired has stopped working, so is no longer active in a job.

clue.text: Going the other way, oddly use "north"

indicators.note: doing something oddly means in a strange, irregular way, so the letters come out of order

blocks.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A contrarian perversely heads north while saying the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' could mean taking odd letters, but here it signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Southern means toward the south, the opposite direction to north.

clue.text: What pairs of clues do, first/second, third/fourth ...

definitions.text: What pairs of clues do, first/second, third/fourth ...

blocks.note: surface reading: a puzzle note about how clues work together, perhaps sharing answers
setter's reading: in this puzzle each pair of clues ends on matching sounds, like lines of a poem

explanation.walkthrough: This clue explains the puzzle's gimmick: read in order, each two clues form a couplet whose last words chime, as 'do' and 'clue' do in 7 and 8 Down.
explanation.definitionFit: Words that end with matching sounds are said to chime with each other, which is what the clue pairs here do.

clue.text: Solver perhaps in a comfortable chair

definitions.note: whimsical: one who is set a puzzle

blocks.note: first meaning: jokingly, the person a setter sets a puzzle for
second meaning: a sofa

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is a joke coinage: if the compiler is the setter, the solver is the one set to, with the -ee ending of employee.
explanation.definitionFit: A settee is an upholstered seat for two or more, a sofa; the -ee pun makes it the puzzle-setter's target.

clue.text: Sire, he's upset: she inherits the prize

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: A father is upset because his daughter, not he, gets the family fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sire' doubles as father in the surface, which makes the inheritance story plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: An heiress is a woman who inherits, or stands to inherit, an estate or fortune.

clue.text: This person's vehicle - maybe repair?

blocks.note: from the setter's view, this person is = I am
a bus is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Someone says their own vehicle might need fixing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repair' is the example, as a word: re-PAIR is a short syllable then a stressed one, the pattern of this metrical foot.
explanation.definitionFit: An iambus or iamb is a metrical foot of one unstressed then one stressed syllable, as in the word repair.

clue.text: He wrote up his name (add initials) in loos

indicators.note: in a down light, up means the letters climb backwards from the bottom
his full name would carry initials too, so those extra letters are the part to strip away

blocks.note: loos are toilets

explanation.surface: A poet scrawls his name on lavatory walls.
explanation.walkthrough: Written backwards, the word for loos becomes the poet's full name with his initials T. S. reversed in front; drop those for the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot was the poet of The Waste Land, a man who wrote, so 'He wrote' points to him.

clue.text: Setter one definite nit, among others

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as me
a means one
definite and sure are synonyms

explanation.surface: The setter is certain to be one of several fools.
explanation.walkthrough: A nit is a unit of luminance (candela per square metre), not a louse egg or a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A nit is one of many units used to quantify things, so it is an example of a unit of quantity.

clue.text: Well-preserved bodies belonging to mothers

definitions.note: a possessive phrase defining a noun, fair because the answer read with an apostrophe, mummies', means exactly belonging to mothers

blocks.note: first meaning: embalmed corpses
second meaning: the possessive of mums

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-preserved' could flatter older women; the word is both Egyptian corpses and, with an apostrophe, mothers' property.
explanation.definitionFit: Mummies are embalmed ancient corpses, and in British usage mummies are also mothers, so mummies' things belong to them.

clue.text: Point caught by article - quickly peruse

blocks.note: south is a compass point
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A briefly read point stuck in a newspaper article.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan a text is to glance over it quickly, looking for key details.

clue.text: Chatter wrecked unirotational gear

indicators.note: something wrecked is smashed apart, so the letters lie scattered

blocks.note: the fodder, letter for letter

explanation.surface: Noisy rattling from a broken one-way gear.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet is a toothed mechanism with a pawl that lets a wheel turn in one direction only.

clue.text: Wipe off a tub - a bird washes here

blocks.note: to dust is to wipe dirt off
a bath is a tub

explanation.surface: Cleaning a tub where a bird bathes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a birdbath, but birds also clean themselves by wallowing in dry earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dust bath is a patch of dry soil where birds flap and roll to rid their feathers of parasites.

clue.text: The theme of this creation, in clever sequestration

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words rather than being built

blocks.note: spans the end of clever and the start of sequestration

explanation.surface: The theme of this puzzle, tucked away cleverly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sequestration' means hiding away, a sly nod to how the answer is concealed.
explanation.definitionFit: Every clue in the puzzle is a line of rhyming poetry, so poetry is its theme.
